claim: A custom microscope allowed simultaneous imaging of the soma and up to 300 μm of contiguous dendrite at 15 Hz while resolving individual spines.
source: A custom microscope allowed us to image the soma and up to 300 μm of contiguous dendrite at 15 Hz, while resolving individual spines.
evidence: The abstract directly states the technical capabilities of the custom microscope used in the study.

claim: The majority of dendritic calcium transients were coincident with global events.
source: The majority of dendritic calcium transients were coincident with global events.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Task-associated calcium signals in dendrites and spines were compartmentalized by dendritic branching.
source: However, task-associated calcium signals in dendrites and spines were compartmentalized by dendritic branching and clustered within branches over approximately 10 μm.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Task-associated calcium signals were clustered within branches over approximately 10 μm.
source: However, task-associated calcium signals in dendrites and spines were compartmentalized by dendritic branching and clustered within branches over approximately 10 μm.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 7.

claim: Diverse behavior-related signals were intermingled and distributed throughout the dendritic arbor.
source: Diverse behavior-related signals were intermingled and distributed throughout the dendritic arbor, potentially supporting a large learning capacity in individual neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Active membrane conductances may produce neurons that integrate input in a point-like, linear manner.
source: Active membrane conductances may simply counteract location-dependent disparities and passive sublinearities across synapses, producing neurons that integrate input in a point-like, linear manner (Bernander et al., 1994; Cash and Yuste, 1999; Spencer and Kandel, 1961).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Active conductances may add nonlinear operations to the input-output transformation of neurons.
source: Alternatively, active conductances may add nonlinear operations to the input-output transformation of neurons.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility discussed in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Back-propagating action potentials can generate widespread calcium transients dependent on firing patterns and synaptic input.
source: Back-propagating action potentials (bAPs) can generate widespread calcium transients, dependent on firing patterns and synaptic input (Jaffe et al., 1992; Magee and Johnston, 1997; Spruston et al., 1995; Waters et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Calcium spikes initiated in the apical tuft generate large and reliable multibranch calcium transients.
source: Calcium spikes initiated in the apical tuft by the conjunction of bAPs and tuft depolarization (Kim and Connors, 1993; Larkum et al., 1999a) generate large and reliable multibranch calcium transients (Helmchen et al., 1999; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Local dendritic spikes can be initiated in individual thin branches and driven by NMDA receptor electrogenesis.
source: In contrast, local dendritic spikes can be initiated in individual thin branches and can be driven by electrogenesis produced by NMDA receptors (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Larkum et al., 2009; Major et al., 2008; Schiller et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2001) and other voltage-gated conductances (Ariav et al., 2003; Golding and Spruston, 1998; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Milojkovic et al., 2005; Nevian et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: A local dendritic spike generates calcium influx that is maximal near sites of coactive synaptic input within its dendrite of origin while calcium influx is minimal or absent at other dendrites.
source: In isolation, a local dendritic spike generates calcium influx that is maximal near sites of coactive synaptic input within its dendrite of origin while calcium influx is minimal or absent at other dendrites (Major et al., 2008; Milojkovic et al., 2007; Schiller et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some studies report a high prevalence of local dendritic spikes during sensory stimulation.
source: Some studies report a high prevalence of local dendritic spikes during sensory stimulation (Palmer et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2013), although the majority of local dendritic spikes were accompanied by somatic spikes (Palmer et al., 2014) and exhibited a sensory selectivity identical to the somatic spikes (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Other studies failed to find local dendritic spikes during sensory stimulation or spontaneous activity.
source: Other studies failed to find local dendritic spikes during sensory stimulation (Svoboda et al., 1997; Svoboda et al., 1999) or spontaneous activity (Hill et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One study suggested that different behaviors trigger calcium transients in nonoverlapping tuft branches.
source: One study suggested that different behaviors trigger calcium transients in nonoverlapping tuft branches (Cichon and Gan, 2015), supporting independent local dendritic operations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Another study found that calcium transients in the dendrites of CA1 neurons were almost always coincident with transients in the soma.
source: However, another study found that calcium transients in the dendrites of CA1 neurons were almost always coincident with transients in the soma (Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015), implying that local dendritic spikes are rare or have a functional selectivity similar to the somatic output.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Clustering of coactive inputs over small length scales could facilitate the generation of local dendritic spikes.
source: Clustering of coactive inputs over small length scales could facilitate the generation of local dendritic spikes (Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Major et al., 2008; Polsky et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some in vivo studies support clustering of functionally similar inputs in dendritic spines of pyramidal neurons.
source: Multiple in vivo studies have probed the selectivity of dendritic spine calcium signals in pyramidal neurons of primary sensory cortex; some of these studies support clustering of functionally similar inputs (Scholl et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2016), while others do not (Chen et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some in vivo studies do not support clustering of functionally similar inputs in dendritic spines of pyramidal neurons.
source: Multiple in vivo studies have probed the selectivity of dendritic spine calcium signals in pyramidal neurons of primary sensory cortex; some of these studies support clustering of functionally similar inputs (Scholl et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2016), while others do not (Chen et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anterior lateral motor (ALM) cortex is critical for decision making and planned directional licking in rodents.
source: Anterior lateral motor (ALM) cortex is critical for decision making and planned directional licking in rodents (Guo et al., 2014b; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons within ALM and connected regions exhibit diverse behavioral selectivity during a tactile decision task.
source: Neurons within ALM (Chen et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2014b) and connected regions (Guo et al., 2017) exhibit diverse behavioral selectivity during a tactile decision task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The microscope provided a 0.35 μm lateral and 1.9 μm axial resolution in the center of the imaging volume.
source: The system provided a 0.35 μm lateral and 1.9 μm axial resolution in the center and 0.56 μm lateral and 4.0 μm axial resolution at the edges of a 525 μm x 525 μm x 300 μm imaging volume.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the microscope system described in the methods.

claim: The microscope provided a 0.56 μm lateral and 4.0 μm axial resolution at the edges of the imaging volume.
source: The system provided a 0.35 μm lateral and 1.9 μm axial resolution in the center and 0.56 μm lateral and 4.0 μm axial resolution at the edges of a 525 μm x 525 μm x 300 μm imaging volume.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the microscope system described in the methods.

claim: Chrna2_OE25-Cre mice expressed in a subpopulation of pyramidal tract (PT) neurons and not intratelencephalic (IT) neurons.
source: Chrna2_OE25-Cre mice expressed in a subpopulation of pyramidal tract (PT) neurons and not intratelencephalic (IT) neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Gerfen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: A total of 3728 spines on 11.4 mm of dendrite from 14 L2/3 neurons were imaged.
source: We imaged a total of 3728 spines on 11.4 mm of dendrite from 14 L2/3 neurons (seven mice; 52 behavioral sessions; per-session medians: 241 trials, 74 spines, 221 μm of dendrite).
evidence: This is a summary of the data collected in the study.

claim: A total of 655 spines on 3.9 mm of dendrite from five L5 neurons were imaged.
source: We imaged a total of 655 spines on 3.9 mm of dendrite from five L5 neurons (four mice; 16 behavioral sessions; per-session medians: 276 trials, 39 spines, 259 μm of dendrite).
evidence: This is a summary of the data collected in the study.

claim: In L2/3 dendrites, independent dendritic activity was rare.
source: In L2/3 dendrites, independent dendritic activity was rare.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: With the somatic threshold set to detecting 1–2 spikes, the probability of independent activity in L2/3 dendrites barely rose above the expected false-positive rate.
source: For example, with the somatic threshold set to detecting 1–2 spikes (~15% ΔF/F; Chen et al., 2013) the probability of independent activity in L2/3 dendrites barely rose above the expected false-positive rate across a range of ΔF/F thresholds (Figure 3C, mean difference at threshold of ΔF/F > 1: 0.037 ± 0.009).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: The proportion of independent activity in spines was higher by one order of magnitude compared to dendrites.
source: In contrast, the proportion of independent activity in spines was higher by one order of magnitude (Figure 3B,C; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for complete co-active, independent, and false positive rate grids).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The proportion of independent activity in spines was close to 30% at thresholds where the false positive rate approached zero.
source: The proportion of independent activity in spines was close to 30%, even at thresholds where the false positive rate approached zero (mean difference at threshold of ΔF/F > 1: 0.324 ± 0.006).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: A higher proportion of independent dendrite activity was observed in L5 tufts compared to L2/3 dendrites.
source: A higher proportion of independent dendrite activity was observed in L5 tufts, compared to L2/3 dendrites (Figure 3C, mean difference at threshold of ΔF/F > 1: 0.15 ± 0.02, p<10−12 Wilcoxon rank-sum test), although the majority of activity was still coincident with the global signal measured in the apical trunk.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3C and statistical testing.

claim: The distribution of independent activity across individual dendrite segments was skewed, especially in L2/3.
source: The distribution of independent activity across individual dendrite segments was skewed, especially in L2/3 (Figure 3D), where the top 10% most independent segments accounted for 76% of all independent activity (versus 35% for L5 dendrite segments; p<0.001 K-S test on distributions).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3D and statistical testing.

claim: In L2/3 dendrites, 63% of spines and 74% of short dendrite segments exhibited significant activity selective for specific trial epochs.
source: In L2/3 dendrites (see Figure 5A–C for an example session), 63% of spines and 74% of short dendrite segments (~3 μm, see Materials and methods) exhibited significant (p<0.01, nonparametric ANOVA and standard error for epoch angle of <30 degrees) activity selective for specific trial epochs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In L2/3 dendrites, 20% of spines and 30% of short dendrite segments exhibited significant selectivity for trial-type during at least one epoch.
source: 20% of spines and 30% of short dendrite segments exhibited significant (p<0.05, permutation test with Bonferroni correction) selectivity for trial-type (right vs. left) during at least one of the epochs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In L5 tuft dendrites, 46% of spines and 39% of dendrite segments were epoch selective.
source: Similar selectivity was observed in L5 tuft dendrites (see Figure 5F–H for an example session; for all sessions: epoch selective: 46% of spines and 39% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 27% of spines and 38% of dendrite segments).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In L5 tuft dendrites, 27% of spines and 38% of dendrite segments were trial-type selective.
source: Similar selectivity was observed in L5 tuft dendrites (see Figure 5F–H for an example session; for all sessions: epoch selective: 46% of spines and 39% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 27% of spines and 38% of dendrite segments).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: After bAP subtraction, 53% of L2/3 spines and 67% of dendrite segments were epoch selective.
source: Similar proportions of spines and dendritic segments with selectivity were observed after bAP subtraction (L2/3, Figure 5D,E, epoch selective: 53% of spines, 67% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 18% of spines and 27% of dendrite segments; L5, Figure 5I,J, epoch selective: 47% of spines, 54% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 28% of spines and 35% of dendrite segments).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data after bAP subtraction.

claim: After bAP subtraction, 18% of L2/3 spines and 27% of dendrite segments were trial-type selective.
source: Similar proportions of spines and dendritic segments with selectivity were observed after bAP subtraction (L2/3, Figure 5D,E, epoch selective: 53% of spines, 67% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 18% of spines and 27% of dendrite segments; L5, Figure 5I,J, epoch selective: 47% of spines, 54% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 28% of spines and 35% of dendrite segments).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data after bAP subtraction.

claim: After bAP subtraction, 47% of L5 spines and 54% of dendrite segments were epoch selective.
source: Similar proportions of spines and dendritic segments with selectivity were observed after bAP subtraction (L2/3, Figure 5D,E, epoch selective: 53% of spines, 67% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 18% of spines and 27% of dendrite segments; L5, Figure 5I,J, epoch selective: 47% of spines, 54% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 28% of spines and 35% of dendrite segments).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data after bAP subtraction.

claim: After bAP subtraction, 28% of L5 spines and 35% of dendrite segments were trial-type selective.
source: Similar proportions of spines and dendritic segments with selectivity were observed after bAP subtraction (L2/3, Figure 5D,E, epoch selective: 53% of spines, 67% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 18% of spines and 27% of dendrite segments; L5, Figure 5I,J, epoch selective: 47% of spines, 54% of dendrite segments, trial-type selective: 28% of spines and 35% of dendrite segments).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data after bAP subtraction.

claim: Epoch selectivity was different for 27% of spine pairs in layer 2/3 dendrite.
source: Epoch selectivity was different (p<0.05, bootstrap across trials) for 27% of spine pairs in layer 2/3 dendrite and 43% of spine pairs in L5 tuft dendrite.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Epoch selectivity was different for 43% of spine pairs in L5 tuft dendrite.
source: Epoch selectivity was different (p<0.05, bootstrap across trials) for 27% of spine pairs in layer 2/3 dendrite and 43% of spine pairs in L5 tuft dendrite.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Pairwise correlations were strongest for nearby dendritic segments and spines in both L2/3 dendrites and L5 tufts.
source: Pairwise correlations were strongest for nearby dendritic segments and spines in both L2/3 dendrites and L5 tufts (Figure 7B,C; p<0.001 for both, nonparametric ANOVA comparison to shuffle).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 7 and statistical testing.

claim: The length constant of the exponential component of signal correlations ranged from 7 to 19 μm.
source: Fits to this exponential-linear function (see Materials and methods), provided estimates of the length constant of the exponential component that ranged from 7 to 19 μm (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Combining across cell types, the length constant was estimated as 8 ± 4 μm for dendrite segments and 13 ± 6 μm for spines.
source: Combining across cell types, we estimated a length constant of 8 ± 4 μm for dendrite segments and 13 ± 6 μm for spines.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding combining data across cell types.

claim: The length constant of noise correlations ranged from 9 to 18 μm.
source: Fits to the exponential-linear function provided estimates of the length constant of the exponential component that ranged from 9 to 18 μm (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Combining across cell types, the length constant of noise correlations was estimated as 10 ± 3 μm for dendrite segments and 14 ± 3 μm for spines.
source: Combining across cell types, we estimated a length constant of 10 ± 3 μm for dendrite segments and 14 ± 3 μm for spines.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding combining data across cell types.

claim: The spatial profile of noise correlations within the dendrite was not significantly different from the profile for signal correlations.
source: Thus, the spatial profile of noise correlations within the dendrite was not significantly different from the profile for signal correlations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the length constants of signal and noise correlations.

claim: Branch location had a significant effect on spine and dendrite pairs from both L2/3 and L5 tuft.
source: We measured the mean signal correlation for spine and dendrite pairs within versus across branches. Branch location had a significant effect on spine and dendrite pairs from both L2/3 and L5 tuft (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 8B.

claim: Correlations were lower when a branch point was crossed for pairs less than 10 μm apart.
source: To selectively test for an influence of branch points, we restricted the data to pairs less than 10 μm apart that were either within a branch or crossed a single branch point. Correlations were lower when a branch point was crossed (Figure 8C; p<0.05 for all groups of pairs except L5 tuft spines).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 8C and statistical testing.

claim: The majority of calcium transients in the dendrites were coincident with global events during task performance.
source: We recorded activity in the dendrites and spines of motor cortex pyramidal neurons as mice performed a tactile discrimination task. The majority of calcium transients in the dendrites were coincident with global events.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Events that were not coincident with global events occurred with higher frequency in the dendritic tufts of L5 neurons than in the dendrites of L2/3 neurons.
source: Events that were not coincident with global events were rare and occurred with higher frequency in the dendritic tufts of L5 neurons than in the dendrites of L2/3 neurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The amplitudes of local calcium signals were modulated by task-related variables and spatially clustered within individual dendritic branches.
source: However, the amplitudes of local calcium signals were modulated by task-related variables and spatially clustered within individual dendritic branches.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 5, 7, and 8.

claim: Sensorimotor signals are compartmentalized within the dendrites of neurons in motor cortex.
source: Our data suggest that sensorimotor signals are compartmentalized within the dendrites of neurons in motor cortex, consistent with models in which branch-specific information enhances the computational or learning capacity of neural circuits (Guerguiev et al., 2017; Poirazi and Mel, 2001; Urbanczik and Senn, 2014; Wu and Mel, 2009).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion, supported by the study's data and consistent with cited theoretical models.

claim: The microscope system uses a voice-coil to move the remote mirror, similar to a large field of view two-photon mesoscope system.
source: The use of a voice-coil to move the remote mirror is similar to a large field of view two-photon mesoscope system (Sofroniew et al., 2016; numerical aperture = 0.6) however, the system described here provides high numerical aperture (1.05), defocuses the beam after the scanning elements, and provides roughly twice the lateral and axial resolution.
evidence: This is a technical comparison to another microscope system, supported by citation.

claim: The system described provides roughly twice the lateral and axial resolution compared to a large field of view two-photon mesoscope system.
source: The use of a voice-coil to move the remote mirror is similar to a large field of view two-photon mesoscope system (Sofroniew et al., 2016; numerical aperture = 0.6) however, the system described here provides high numerical aperture (1.05), defocuses the beam after the scanning elements, and provides roughly twice the lateral and axial resolution.
evidence: This is a technical comparison to another microscope system, supported by citation.

claim: Inferred correlations between input (spines) and output (soma) did not reliably predict true correlations in computer simulations.
source: Computer simulations indicated that conclusions drawn from this approach are limited (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Inferred correlations between input (spines) and output (soma) did not reliably predict true correlations, even in simple and linear models of the relationship between activity and fluorescence signals in dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a finding from computer simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence or absence of structured correlations was accurately detected using the bAP subtraction approach in simulations.
source: Using our subtraction methods on simulated data, the presence or absence of structured correlations was accurately detected and the inferred length scale of pairwise correlations closely matched the simulated scale.
evidence: This is a finding from computer simulations described in the discussion.

claim: The inferred length scale of pairwise correlations closely matched the simulated scale using the bAP subtraction approach.
source: Using our subtraction methods on simulated data, the presence or absence of structured correlations was accurately detected and the inferred length scale of pairwise correlations closely matched the simulated scale.
evidence: This is a finding from computer simulations described in the discussion.

claim: The length scales estimated could reflect pre- and post-synaptic processes.
source: The length scales we estimate could reflect pre- and post-synaptic processes and should thus be regarded as a description of the local component of calcium signals in the dendrite.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the limitations of the methods.

claim: Another study in motor cortex reported that at least 95% of calcium spikes in the L5 tuft were not shared across sibling branches during a forced-running paradigm.
source: In contrast, another study in motor cortex reported that at least 95% of calcium spikes in the L5 tuft were not shared across sibling branches during a forced-running paradigm (Cichon and Gan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The results are similar to studies in sensory cortex and hippocampus where the majority of dendritic spikes are coincident with the generation of somatic spikes.
source: Our results, however, are similar to studies in sensory cortex (Smith et al., 2013) and hippocampus (Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015), in which the majority of dendritic spikes are coincident with the generation of somatic spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ALM is a key hub in a multi-regional neural circuit that sustains memory-related activity.
source: ALM is a key hub in a multi-regional neural circuit that sustains memory-related activity (Guo et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Sustained activity in ALM is internally maintained by attractor dynamics in recurrent connections involving ALM, thalamus and other brain regions.
source: This sustained activity is internally maintained by attractor dynamics in recurrent connections (Inagaki et al., 2019), involving ALM, thalamus (Guo et al., 2017) and other brain regions (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biophysical models have shown that maintenance of memory-related activity requires time constants of excitation that outlast feedback inhibition.
source: Biophysical models have shown that maintenance of memory-related activity requires time constants of excitation that outlast feedback inhibition (Wang, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Long-lasting dendritic excitation could be part of the cellular mechanism of short-term memory.
source: Long-lasting dendritic excitation could be part of the cellular mechanism of short-term memory.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the context of short-term memory.

claim: In ex vivo and in vivo experiments, the peak depolarization and calcium influx generated by local dendritic spikes are comparable or larger than the peaks generated by a bAP or calcium spike.
source: In ex vivo (Antic et al., 2010; Golding et al., 2002; Milojkovic et al., 2007; Nevian et al., 2007) and in vivo (Svoboda et al., 1999) experiments, however, the peak depolarization and calcium influx generated by local dendritic spikes are comparable or larger than the peaks generated by a bAP or calcium spike.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Artificial generation of a local dendritic spike on a single branch does not reliably drive somatic action potentials or calcium spikes.
source: Artificial generation of a local dendritic spike on a single branch does not reliably drive somatic action potentials or calcium spikes (Larkum et al., 2009; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Palmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During the tactile decision task, local dendritic spikes are either very rare or are almost always part of a synchronized, multi-branch depolarization of the dendrites that reliably drives somatic action potentials or calcium spikes.
source: Hence, our results suggest that during the tactile decision task, local dendritic spikes are either very rare or are almost always part of a synchronized, multi-branch depolarization of the dendrites that reliably drives somatic action potentials or calcium spikes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and prior literature.

claim: The rarity of independent local dendritic spiking does not preclude functional compartmentalization within the dendrite.
source: The rarity of independent local dendritic spiking does not preclude functional compartmentalization within the dendrite.
evidence: This is a clarification of the implications of the findings.

claim: Local synaptic input may modulate the depolarization and calcium influx into the dendritic shaft produced by bAPs or calcium spikes.
source: Local synaptic input may modulate the depolarization and calcium influx into the dendritic shaft produced by bAPs or calcium spikes (Larkum et al., 1999b; Stuart and Häusser, 2001; Waters et al., 2003), as well as the probability of coincident local dendritic spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Individual dendrites of sensory cortex neurons receive inputs with diverse feature selectivity.
source: Individual dendrites of sensory cortex neurons receive inputs with diverse feature selectivity (Chen et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2011; Jia et al., 2010; Scholl et al., 2017; Varga et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mapping the diversity of functional input to individual neurons in frontal cortex is critical to understand decision-making, motor planning, and short-term memory.
source: Mapping the diversity of functional input to individual neurons in frontal cortex is critical to understand decision-making, motor planning, and short-term memory (Inagaki et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The short exponential decay of distance-dependent correlations could reflect a clustering of pre-synaptic inputs with similar functional properties or input onto nearby spines from the same axon.
source: The short exponential decay of distance-dependent correlations could reflect a clustering of pre-synaptic inputs with similar functional properties or input onto nearby spines from the same axon (Bloss et al., 2018; Kasthuri et al., 2015; Knott et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The length constant (~10 μm) is similar to a number of spatially restricted plasticity mechanisms.
source: The length constant (~10 μm) is similar to a number of spatially restricted plasticity mechanisms.
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's findings to known plasticity mechanisms.

claim: When activated by stimulation of a single spine, small GTPases spread throughout ~5–10 μm of the dendrite and influence plasticity at nearby spines.
source: When activated by stimulation of a single spine, small GTPases spread throughout ~5–10 μm of the dendrite (Harvey et al., 2008; Murakoshi et al., 2011; Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015) and influence plasticity at nearby spines (Harvey and Svoboda, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During development, ryanodine-sensitive calcium release and BDNF-mediated synaptic depression can produce selective stabilization of inputs with similar spontaneous activity over distances of 5–10 μm.
source: During development, ryanodine-sensitive calcium release (Lee et al., 2016) and BDNF-mediated synaptic depression (Winnubst et al., 2015) can produce selective stabilization of inputs with similar spontaneous activity over distances of 5–10 μm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The length scale is consistent with the high calcium zone produced by local dendritic spikes.
source: This length scale is also consistent with the high calcium zone produced by local dendritic spikes (Major et al., 2008) and subthreshold nonlinear NMDA receptor-mediated amplification of synaptic calcium signals by the activity of neighboring spines (Harnett et al., 2012; Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Correlations exhibited a linear decay over longer distances (up to 180 μm) in addition to a short exponential decay.
source: We found that in addition to a short exponential decay, correlations exhibited a linear decay over longer distances (up to 180 μm).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of pairwise correlations.

claim: The linear decay may reflect a combination of multiple processes, including passive and active attenuation of subthreshold potentials and locally initiated dendritic spikes.
source: This decay may reflect a combination of multiple processes, including passive and active (via voltage-gated potassium channels) attenuation of both subthreshold potentials and locally initiated dendritic spikes (Gasparini et al., 2004; Harnett et al., 2013; Major et al., 2008; Milojkovic et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A number of mechanisms could confine excitability in branch-specific manner, including current sinks towards branch points, the sub-branch organization of inhibitory input, and the distribution of Kv4.2 potassium channels.
source: A number of mechanisms could confine excitability in branch-specific manner, including current sinks towards branch points (Branco et al., 2010; Marlin and Carter, 2014; Müllner et al., 2015), the sub-branch organization of inhibitory input (Bloss et al., 2016), and the distribution of Kv4.2 potassium channels (Losonczy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compartmentalization may reflect local dendritic operations that expand the processing capacity of individual neurons.
source: This compartmentalization may reflect local dendritic operations that expand the processing capacity of individual neurons (Archie and Mel, 2000; Poirazi and Mel, 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Local operations may play a critical role in learning.
source: These local operations may also play a critical role in learning (Frick et al., 2004; Guerguiev et al., 2017; Losonczy et al., 2008; Urbanczik and Senn, 2014), and future work in the motor cortex could explore the relationship between compartmentalized anatomical changes in the dendrite (Chen et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2009) and clustered task-related activity during learning.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The microscope uses two mirror galvanometers and a remote focusing system to steer 16 kHz scan lines arbitrarily in three dimensions.
